area: mac4DSTEM/App/ — workflow state, recovery, residency, ACOM workflow (excluding AppState.swift)
summary: This area is unusually disciplined and most of what it claims about itself is true. The eight extracted seams (DatasetResidency, LoadedView, PendingLoad, SessionReplay, SessionGates, StrainProduct, QCalibrationRun, ReplayRun) each own their state AND their transitions behind `private(set)` with an explicit reset/clear and a written list of the paths that must call it; DatasetResidency's generation counter and ReplayRun's derived `phase` are real defences against late-landing async publishes, not decoration. ReplayPlan is the strongest file here: the parser is total, an unknown key/kind/role refuses by name rather than defaulting, and `ReplayRecordFrameMap` refuses any value with no exact re-expression instead of rounding. `RecordedSpecificationOutcome`'s three-case split, the `.withoutMounting` + `unmountedVolumeName(forBookmark:)` pairing in both bookmark resolvers, `StrainProduct.originProvenance` snapshotted at publish rather than at export, `DatasetRecoveryRecord.position(inViewWith:)` refusing rather than clamping across frames, and the honest `ResidencyAdmission.measuredWorkingSetFraction = nil` are all correct and correctly explained. What I found is concentrated in three places: one regression guard that cannot fail, three comments that no longer describe the code, and the recovery record's write path, which lacks the dataset-identity check its own read path performs. Two smaller notes not raised as findings: `LoadedView.scanIndexedResultsWereCleared` (App/LoadedView.swift:41) has zero readers anywhere in the repo despite a name that asserts an action was taken; and `PromoteRunCaption` (UI/DatasetInspector.swift:447) calls `ReplayPlanner.plan` inside a SwiftUI view body, which is parsing in a View and against the repo's "Views describe UI only" hard rule, though it is cheap and produces no wrong number.

findings.title: S7's iDPC-remedy regression guard asserts a string that exists nowhere, so it cannot fail
findings.why: `XCTAssertFalse(refusal?.contains("enter the scale manually") == true)` guards the Gate B finding of 2026-08-25: physical iDPC must NOT print the Q surface's manual-scale remedy, because manual scale entry provably cannot restore physical iDPC. But the literal "enter the scale manually" appears in no production string. The only manual-scale remedy the app emits is `Calibration.swift:755` — " Enter the reciprocal pixel size manually to proceed — that bypasses this fit." — capital E and entirely different wording. The substring occurs only in prose comments (Calibration.swift:691, AppState.swift:4466) and in this test's own comment at line 104. The assertion is therefore false-by-construction on every possible value of `refusal`, including nil.
findings.failureScenario: Mutate `AppState.idpcOriginFitRefusal` (AppState.swift:4469) from `calibration.originFitJudgement.map { ... }` back to `calibration.originFitRefusal` — the exact pre-S7 defect this test was written to pin. Line 100 still passes (the judgement contains "probe radius"), line 108 still passes (`originFitRefusal` is `judgement + diagnosis + remedy`, so it contains the judgement verbatim), and line 113 still passes because `originFitRefusal` contains "Enter the reciprocal pixel size manually", not "enter the scale manually". The whole suite stays green while the DPC controls tell the user to enter the scale manually to restore quantitative iDPC — advice that cannot work. This is the repo's stated #1 failure mode ("break every new test before trusting it") reaching a science-adjacent surface.

findings.title: reciprocalMetrologyRefusal's fittedMaps/recordedMean branch is unreachable and fails OPEN; its comment claims the opposite
findings.why: The comment says "Reachable: `originSupportsReciprocalMetrology` also fails when the fit is not sane, and then the refusal above has already returned. If it did not, say something rather than nothing." Neither half holds. Reachability: line 86 is entered only when `originSupportsReciprocalMetrology` is false; with kind in {fittedMaps, recordedMean} that requires `originFitIsSane == false` (Calibration.swift:607), which requires `origin?.rmsResidual != nil` and `probeRadius != nil` (Calibration.swift:570). `judgedOriginResidual` is literally `origin?.rmsResidual` (Calibration.swift:580), so it is non-nil whenever `originFitIsSane` is false, so `originFitJudgement` (Calibration.swift:696) is non-nil, so `originFitRefusal` is non-nil, so line 91 always returns first. The branch is dead. Behaviour if it were reached: it returns `originQuantitativeRefusal(for: calibration)`, which line 91 just proved is nil — so it returns nil, i.e. GRANTS the reciprocal measurement that `originSupportsReciprocalMetrology` refused. It says nothing, not "something rather than nothing", and a gate whose default is admit is the inverse of the release's refusal rule quoted in this file's own header (lines 23-25).
findings.failureScenario: Any future change that makes `originFitIsSane` false without producing a judgement re-arms this. The exact shape is already documented in Calibration.swift:770-779: a NaN fitted map returns kind `.fittedMaps` with no residual beside it. Today `meanOrigin`'s finiteness check (Calibration.swift:786) keeps that out. Remove or weaken that check — or add any third sanity condition to `originFitIsSane` that does not also produce a judgement string — and `AppState.calibrateQFromCrystal` (AppState.swift:5021) receives nil from this gate, measures a Q pixel scale from an unmeasured origin, and stamps it `.measuredInApp`: S13 E1 measured that substitution at 1.14 px on sim_Au and 7.07 px on downsample_Si_SiGe_exp, which is the failure this gate was built to close structurally. No test can cover the branch, so nothing would catch it.

findings.title: persistRecoveryPosition writes the current dataset's position and frame into the PREVIOUS dataset's recovery record
findings.why: (Defect line is in the excluded file, but this is recovery correctness, the named focus of this area; the type it corrupts is App/WorkspaceRecovery.swift.) The guard is `guard descriptor != nil, var record = recoveryRecord` — it checks that SOME dataset is open, never that `record.datasetID` is the dataset now open. It then overwrites `selectedX/Y`, `analysisMode` and `loadSpecification` from live state and persists. The read side does perform exactly that identity check: `activate` compares `recovery.datasetID` against the descriptor's standardized path (AppState.swift:2633) before applying anything. The window in which the two disagree is wide and real: `activate` sets `self.descriptor` at AppState.swift:2367, while `recoveryRecord` is not replaced until `rememberOpenedDataset(url)` at AppState.swift:2326 — deliberately deferred until after `await runCurrentAnalysis()`, i.e. after the whole-cube pass, which on a multi-GB cube is minutes. The scan-position sliders (UI/ContentView.swift:136-143) and the arrow-key handler (UI/ContentView.swift:1182) are gated only on `descriptor != nil` and workspace area, not on `isLoadingDataset`, and `activate` forces `workspaceArea = .prepare` (AppState.swift:2621). So `selectScan` -> `persistRecoveryPosition()` is live throughout that window.
findings.failureScenario: Dataset A (a scan-cropped session) has been opened and remembered. The user opens dataset B at full extent and, while B's first whole-cube pass runs, drags the scan-position slider. `persistRecoveryPosition` persists {datasetID: A, bookmark: A, selectedX/Y: B's position, loadSpecification: B's full-extent spec}. Next launch, File ▸ Reopen resolves A's bookmark and opens A with its recorded crop restored; `DatasetRecoveryRecord.position(inViewWith:)` (App/WorkspaceRecovery.swift:131) compares the record's now-full-extent `scanCrop` (nil) against A's restored crop, and — if the user had instead been on a full-extent A, the common case — the frames compare equal and B's scan position is applied to A verbatim. That is precisely the "defensible pixel the user never chose" that S5 built the frame stamp to prevent, entering through a door the stamp cannot see because the stamp itself was written from the wrong dataset.

findings.title: LoadedView's header claims its display surface has no reader; three of the four things it names are rendered by the inspector
findings.why: Lines 45-52 read "**NOT YET SHOWN ANYWHERE.** Nothing in `UI/` reads this type's display surface — not this, not `summary`, not `binningNotice`, not `invalidatedCalibration`. ... the wiring belongs with L5's configurator". L5 landed. `UI/DatasetInspector.swift:69` renders `summary`, `:74` renders `binningNotice`, `:175` renders `invalidatedCalibration`, and `discardedDetectorRows/Columns` — the property this comment is attached to — reaches the screen through both `summary` (LoadedView.swift:112-114) and `binningNotice` (LoadedView.swift:138-142). The inspector even says so in the past tense at DatasetInspector.swift:62: "`LoadedView`'s whole display surface had no reader." This file was never updated. The repo's hard rule is "No claim stands that a reader cannot reproduce" and this file's own sibling (App/RecentDatasets.swift:19-23) documents correcting exactly this class of stale header claim.
findings.failureScenario: A session picking up L5/S4 follow-on work reads this header, concludes the binning notice and the invalidated-calibration list are still invisible, and wires a second rendering path for them — producing a duplicated notice, or (worse) concludes the app never states the bin² intensity consequence and adds a competing wording that can drift from LoadedView.binningNotice. The inverse error is equally available: a reviewer auditing "is the reduced-view provenance shown?" trusts the header and records a false gap in docs/open-items.md. The comment is the only documentation of this type's contract with UI/, and it is wrong about three of four properties.

findings.title: A single unreadable recents entry silently discards all eight, and the next open persists the loss
findings.why: `decode` swallows every decoding error with `try?` and `recent()` (line 147) turns that into `[]`. `[RecentDataset]` decodes all-or-nothing, so one malformed element — a `lastOpened` the decoder rejects, a truncated `bookmark`, or any future required field added to `RecentDataset` (line 3-8) — silently yields an empty list rather than the seven good entries. `RecentDatasets.init` (App/RecentDatasets.swift:47) adopts that empty list, and the first `remember()` (line 56-63) calls `save()` -> `persist(entries)` -> `WorkspaceRecoveryStore.saveRecent`, overwriting the stored blob with a one-element list. The loss is then permanent. Each lost entry carries a security-scoped bookmark that is the ONLY way this sandboxed app can reach that file without a fresh open panel (the app holds `files.user-selected.read-write` only — see App/SessionSidecarLocator.swift:38-46). Note the layer above already anticipates corrupt stored data: `RecentDatasets.relabel` (line 95-101) was hardened against "a corrupted or hand-edited blob" reaching init — but this `try?` guarantees only a *structurally valid* corrupt blob ever gets that far, so the partial-corruption case has no handling at all.
findings.failureScenario: A future build adds a non-optional field to `RecentDataset` (or a user's defaults blob is partially damaged — the repo has already had UserDefaults emptied wholesale once, by the 2026-08-14 bundle-identifier change recorded as C10). On next launch the welcome screen shows an empty recents list with no message. The user re-opens one dataset through the panel; `remember` persists a single-entry list and the other seven paths and grants are gone. There is no error, no status line, and no way for the user to tell an empty list from a wiped one. The fix is per-element decoding (decode `[JSONValue]` or `[FailableDecodable<RecentDataset>]` and keep what survives) plus a status line when entries were dropped.

findings.title: A stale recents bookmark is re-created outside its security scope and the failure is swallowed
findings.why: (Defect line is in the excluded file; the App/ API it misuses is `WorkspaceRecoveryStore.bookmark(for:)`, App/WorkspaceRecovery.swift:154.) `openRecent` resolves the bookmark (AppState.swift:2082) and, when `stale` is true, calls `refreshStoredBookmark` at line 2084 — BEFORE `openFile` -> `openFileAsync` starts the security scope at AppState.swift:2273. Creating a `.withSecurityScope` bookmark for a URL resolved from a security-scoped bookmark requires that scope to be active in a sandboxed app. The sibling path does exactly that: `SessionSidecarLocator.grant` calls `url.startAccessingSecurityScopedResource()` (App/SessionSidecarLocator.swift:182) before `remember(url, forSourcePath:)` on the stale branch (line 184). The recents path does not, and `refreshStoredBookmark`'s `try?` means the caller cannot tell a refused re-bookmark from a successful one.
findings.failureScenario: A dataset is moved or its volume is re-created, making its stored bookmark stale-but-resolvable. Every subsequent open from Recents resolves it, reports stale, attempts the refresh outside the scope, fails, swallows the error, and stores nothing — so the entry is never repaired. When the bookmark finally stops resolving entirely, `openRecent`'s catch (AppState.swift:2100-2103) deletes the entry and tells the user "no longer accessible", for a file that was reachable on every previous open. Nothing anywhere records that the repair had been failing silently for weeks. Confirming this needs a run (a sandboxed build, a deliberately staled bookmark, and a check of whether `bookmarkData` throws); the asymmetry against SessionSidecarLocator.swift:182 is the evidence that it should not be relied on unguarded either way.
